elite.lede: Elite Indo-Pak Restaurant is an Indian and Pakistani restaurant in Sugar Land, Texas. Markit Media built its website, produced a website showcase reel and a social media reel, and designed a set of dish-led social posts that share one dark, gold-accented look.
elite.deliverables: Website, website showcase reel, social media reel, 12 social posts shown on this page

sections.heading: The challenge
paragraphs: Elite opened in 2022 in Sugar Land, Texas. On its own website it describes the aim as presenting Indian and Pakistani cooking as a refined, modern dining experience, with online ordering, catering and private events alongside the dining room.

The menu is built on dishes many guests already know: karahi, tikka, samosas, daal gosht, ras malai. That is a visual problem as much as a marketing one. Familiar food, often served in rich sauces, has to look as polished online as the restaurant says it is, and it has to do so in a feed where every other restaurant is also posting food.

sections.heading: Our approach
paragraphs: We started from the restaurant's own positioning and kept one look across the website and the social posts: dark backgrounds, warm gold lettering and a single dish at the centre of each frame.

Every post carries the Elite mark at the top, and the dish posts share the same footer, a reservation phone number and the website address, so each one works on its own as an invitation to book. Dishes sit on dark surfaces such as marble, wood and slate, which keeps the colour in the food instead of the background.

Headlines pair a script face for the feeling ("Satisfy your Desi Cravings", "Devour the Goodness") with a plain serif for the supporting line. Thin arrow call-outs name each dish, for example Karahi Qeema, Chicken Tikka Boti or Peshawari Karahi, so viewers learn the menu while they scroll.

sections.heading: What we delivered
paragraphs: The work spans the website, two videos and a run of social posts. The posts shown further down this page cover starters, mains, desserts and a catering offer.

sections.heading: Lessons for restaurant brands
bullets: Name the dish on the image. A small call-out label turns a food photo into a menu preview and helps guests who do not know a dish by sight.
Put the booking route on the post. A phone number and web address in the same place each time means a dish post does not depend on its caption to be useful.
Style offers like dishes. The catering post uses the same logo and headline treatment as the menu posts, so an offer reads as part of the brand rather than an ad dropped into the feed.

cambridge-electrical.lede: Cambridge Electrical Appliances sells home, kitchen and personal-care appliances in Pakistan under the Cambridge Appliances name. sections.heading: The challenge
paragraphs: Cambridge sells across many appliance categories. Its website lists home appliances such as dry irons, fan heaters and insect killers, hair and beauty tools, and a wide kitchen range of blenders, juicers, food processors, ovens and cookware.

A catalogue that wide is hard to post about without every post looking different. The creative needed one recognisable system that could carry a hair dryer, a wok set and a vacuum flask, show the product clearly, and still change with the season.

sections.heading: Our approach
paragraphs: Every post uses the same frame. The Cambridge mark and its line "Your Family Member" sit at the top, a large headline names the benefit or the moment, the product fills the middle, and the footer carries the model number and the website address.

Small red and white icon badges such as Durable, Lightweight, Easy to use and Non-stick give the key features at a glance without a paragraph of copy. Headlines play on the product: "Blowout" for a hair dryer, "To-asty snack?" for a toaster, "Flip with confidence" for a kitchen tong.

Everyday product posts stay on neutral grey and white backgrounds. The summer series changes the system: pink, yellow, teal and green backgrounds, fruit, palm leaves, parasols and a shared #summerdelights tag turn the same blenders and juicers into a seasonal campaign.

sections.heading: Lessons for appliance brands
bullets: Lead with the moment, not the model. Headlines about a morning, a snack or a season give the product a reason to be in the feed; the model number can sit quietly in the footer.
Show features as icons. Two or three badges beat a paragraph on a social post and keep the layout consistent from product to product.
Let the season change the background, not the system. The summer posts look different but share the same logo position, headline weight and footer, so they still read as Cambridge.

sections.heading: What the posts had to do
paragraphs: An agency's own feed is its portfolio, so these posts aim at the people who buy marketing: they should be recognisable to a marketer, funny enough to be shared and good enough to show the standard of the work. Each series turns a familiar piece of marketing life into a short, visual joke.

sections.heading: The series
paragraphs: The first series asks "What if" a well-known screen character was in digital marketing. Each post cuts the character out over a colour-graded backdrop, repeats the same headline and gives the character one line of marketing advice about click-through rate, vanity metrics, algorithms, trust, audience relationships, sustainable growth, ROI and discounts. These posts use stills of film and television characters, which this page describes without naming. Whether the agency holds the rights to use them has not been confirmed.

A second series gives everyday objects eyes and lips: a laptop, a phone and a keyboard that talk back. The speech bubbles carry the jokes, such as a phone with no storage left for 3,782 selfies and a keyboard tired of mistyped words.

A third series treats fonts as characters. Helvetica becomes the confident brand strategist and Times New Roman the traditional copywriter, each as an illustrated figure on a grid with short personality notes. A fourth series is a set of ad-platform in-jokes on mustard and pink sticky notes, about a performance review run by an ad platform, a raise that fails because a budget limit was not met, feedback that is only scheduled for later and reach that has decreased.

The last series is called What's on our desks. It lists the objects on the desks of a senior social media manager, a junior social media manager, a manager, a graphic designer and a web developer, with hand-lettered labels and arrows on a dark green or orange torn-paper background.

sections.heading: The look
paragraphs: The Markit Media logo, a stylised M in slashes beside the name, sits at the top, and the footer is the agency's social handle. Each series has its own palette and type treatment, but all of them are built from large headlines, cut-out imagery and a single joke per post.

sections.heading: How this differs from Logo Folio

fashion-feed.lede: Fashion Feed is the collection of social media designs Markit Media has made for fashion and apparel brands: promotional sale posts, occasion-wear and menswear campaigns, and lifestyle posts for sleepwear, from three clients.

sections.heading: What this collection shows
paragraphs: Fashion social media is a mix of three jobs, and this collection has an example of each. Sale posts turn a discount into a clear headline, with a badge and a button. Collection posts let the clothing carry the picture, with a short line and an ordering route. Lifestyle posts sell a mood: a lazy Sunday, a slumber party, a winter spent in bed.

The 40 pieces come from three clients: Find My Apparel, with teal and lime sale posts; Minhaz Couture, with peach and teal posts for embroidered women's suits and menswear; and Easywear, with pattern-matched backgrounds for pyjama sets.

sections.heading: How to use this page
paragraphs: This page is the gallery. If you want to see how one brand's feed worked as a system, with its identity, its colours and the reasoning behind each post, open that client's own case study from the list below. If you are comparing ways to present clothing on social media, start with the filters in the gallery and open the posts that look closest to your own range.

foodfolio.lede: FoodFolio is the collection of social media designs Markit Media has made for restaurants, cafés, caterers and food brands: dish-led menu posts, seasonal and festival campaigns, offers and product posts, from eight clients.

sections.heading: What this collection shows
paragraphs: Food design starts with the photograph and then has to carry a message, a price or a booking route around it. The 114 pieces here show several ways to do that: a dark, gold-accented menu series for a Sugar Land restaurant, flame-lit steakhouse posts for two Texas locations, Ramadan iftar and Eid campaigns, a caterer's event-by-event series, juice-bar coupons, pizza and fries offers with was-and-now prices, seasonal jerky bundles and a supplier's quizzes and product posts.
The eight clients are Elite, Tourão Brazilian Steakhouse, Sheesha Lounge and Grill, Pakhlanze, Pizza Warma, Qwench Juice Bar, Wild Game Jerky and Chefiality.

paragraphs: This page is the gallery of food and beverage creative. logo-folio.lede: Logo Folio is Markit Media's collection of logo design and logo animation: the marks themselves, with their colours, typefaces and applications, for more than thirty brands, plus a set of animated logos.

sections.heading: What this collection shows
paragraphs: Each board in the gallery shows one mark and the decisions around it: the symbol and the wordmark, the colour codes, the typefaces and a few applications such as a sign, a tag, a polo shirt or a phone icon. The set ranges from monograms and lettermarks to illustrated emblems, Urdu calligraphy, portrait marks and a mark built from a ring and a diamond.

The animations at the top show how some of the marks move: a logo reveal for an energy company, a technology brand, a food supplier, a fashion label, a caterer, a fresh-produce brand and a creative agency.

sections.heading: How this differs from Branding and Visual Identity
paragraphs: Logo Folio is about the mark and its movement, and it includes every board in the portfolio. The Branding and Visual Identity page is narrower: it presents a smaller group of complete identity systems, where the logo is shown working across stationery, packaging, signage and screens. If you need to see how a brand works in use, start there; if you want to compare logo ideas, start here.

social-media-designs.lede: Social Media Designs is the cross-industry collection of social posts Markit Media has designed: more than 290 pieces for 25 brands across healthcare, technology, retail, household products, sport, beauty and professional services.

sections.heading: What this collection shows
paragraphs: The collection is organised by the work itself rather than by one client. It shows how social post design changes with the job: educational carousels and in-jokes for marketers, supportive quote posts for a treatment centre, product catalogues for appliances, flasks and hardware, sports team reveals and match-day posts, launch teasers and festival greetings.

Repeated systems are the common thread. Whatever the industry, each brand gets a logo position, a headline style, a colour pair and a footer that repeat from post to post, so the feed reads as one brand.

everest-snacks.lede: Everest Snacks is an energy bar brand that describes itself as backed by Shahi. In 2026 Markit Media worked on its digital presence on several fronts: we designed and developed its website, everestsnacks.com, and we also handled its social media, photography, AI enhancement of photos and animation.

sections.heading: What we did for Everest
paragraphs: Our work for Everest covered five areas. The website is public, so it is described in detail below and can be checked. The other four areas are described by what they are, because we are not publishing counts, dates or figures for them.

sections.heading: The website at a glance
paragraphs: The site opens with one short message, "Fuel your adventure". It shows the four flavours as cards, places four trust claims under the headline and points shoppers to where the bars are sold.

The brand name sets the theme. The site's FAQ explains that Everest Energy Bars are inspired by Mount Everest, the highest peak in the world, so the mountain runs through the copy, from "a mountain of energy in every bite" to the last of the five values, "Never stop climbing".

sections.heading: The home page
paragraphs: The home page opens with the headline "Fuel your adventure", one line of supporting copy and an "Explore Bars" button. Directly beneath sits a strip of four short claims: premium quality, best value, nationwide availability and "Shahi trusted", which the site backs with the line "True to our promise. Backed by Shahi."

Further down, an "Our Energy Bars" row shows the four flavours, a "Goodness in every bite" row pairs the product with five everyday goals (hiking higher, working harder, living better, training stronger, going further), and a "Loved by our community" slider carries testimonials from three named customers.

A tabbed where-to-buy block follows, split into local modern trade, international modern trade and online stores, each showing retailer logos, and a "Follow us on Instagram" block shows three posts. A newsletter sign-up, "Stay energized", sits above the footer on every page.

sections.heading: The four bars
paragraphs: The Products page gives each bar its own card: the flavour name in capitals, a short description in the brand's own words, and protein and energy badges.
bullets: Salted Caramel: smooth caramel with a touch of sea salt. Simply irresistible.
Peanut Butter Chocolate: chocolatey crunch with rich and wholesome peanuts.
Peanut Butter Choco Royale: rich chocolate with peanut butter and wholesome oats.
Caramel Indulgence: decadent caramel with nuts and a hint of exotic vanilla.

sections.heading: Why Everest and Connect With Us
paragraphs: The Why Everest page opens with a banner ("Real ingredients. Real energy. Made to fuel real everyday.") and a message from the founder, then lists five values (people first, grow every day, do what's right, built to perform, never stop climbing). A five-step "Everest Journey" graphic, from ingredients to impact, and a ten-question FAQ close the page.

The contact page is aimed at a specific audience, university students. Besides name, email and phone, the form asks what the message is about, with two options, Final Year Project (FYP) and Campus Ambassador, then the university, an optional semester and message, and a file upload for a project.

sections.heading: Photography and AI-enhanced images
paragraphs: Photography and AI enhancement of photos were part of our work for Everest. On the site, pictures do much of the talking: the home page opens on a lifestyle photograph of a man with the bars, each flavour has its own product image with its protein and energy badges, the Why Everest and Connect With Us pages open on illustrated banners, and each blog card carries an illustrated graphic.
We credit no individual picture here. The disciplines are ours; which image came from which step is not part of this page.

sections.heading: Social media and animation
paragraphs: Social media and animation were also part of our work. The site connects to the brand's channels: the "Follow us on Instagram" block on the home page links to the brand's account, @everestsnack, and shows three posts, a sports-themed post for Salted Caramel, a Father's Day post and a lifestyle post of someone opening a bar.

sections.heading: The blog
paragraphs: Three articles are dated 30 July 2026, each roughly 600 to 800 words: "Why Natural Ingredients Matter in Healthy Snacks", "Are Energy Bars Good for Weight Management?" and "Healthy Snacks vs. Energy Bars: Which Is Better?" They take on questions a shopper might ask before choosing a snack, and they are published from Markit Media's account.

sections.heading: How it was built
paragraphs: The site runs on WordPress with Elementor Pro on the Astra theme. Its pages are dated July 2026: the home page on 20 July and the others by 30 July. The footer credits Markit Media as designer and developer of the site, with a link to our site, and lists a phone number, an email address and a Karachi address. The footer credit covers the website; the social media, photography, AI photo enhancement and animation work is described from our own project record.

sections.heading: What to take from it
paragraphs: Put the claims next to the headline. On desktop, Everest's four trust claims sit directly under the headline, inside the first screen.
Keep product descriptions short. Each bar has a flavour name and a brief description, in the same shape across the range.
Show who you want to hear from. The contact form's student-specific options, Final Year Project and Campus Ambassador, make that plain.
Answer the buying questions in one place. The ten-question FAQ covers flavours, storage and where to buy on a single page.
Connect the site to the social channels. The home page's Instagram block shows three posts and links to the brand's account.
